Why kiln-dried oak moves less than air-dried

By Ruth Ellery, published 2 February 2026

Every piece of solid oak moves with the humidity of the room around it. How much it moves, and whether that movement opens a joint, is decided long before the timber reaches a workshop.

What drying actually removes

Freshly sawn oak carries free water in the cell cavities and bound water in the cell walls. Removing the free water costs nothing in dimension. It is the bound water, below roughly thirty percent moisture content, whose loss makes the timber shrink.

Where a kiln differs from a stack

Air drying in a covered stack settles at whatever the local climate allows, which in northern England is around sixteen to eighteen percent. A kiln takes the same boards down to eight to ten percent under controlled temperature and humidity, which is close to the equilibrium moisture content of a heated room.

Why it matters indoors

A table built at eighteen percent and then installed beside a radiator keeps drying after it is finished, and that shrinkage has to go somewhere. Building at ten percent means the remaining seasonal movement is small enough for ordinary joinery to absorb. The Timber Research EMC tables set out the expected figures by region, and the Institute drying standard gives the tolerances we build to.
